opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, robotics is fundamentally a full-stack problem, and that's why NVIDIA is approaching it as a platform rather than a single product. There are really three computers you need to build intelligent robots.

The first is the computer you use to train the brain, the large-scale GPU infrastructure where you train foundation models for robots. That's where projects like our humanoid foundation model work come in. We want a generalist model that can take in vision, language, and proprioception and output motor actions, much like what large language models did for text.

The second is the simulation computer. Data is the biggest bottleneck in robotics. You can't scrape motor control data off the internet the way you scrape text. So simulation becomes essential. With tools like Isaac Sim and Omniverse, we can run physics thousands of times faster than real time, randomize environments, and generate huge amounts of synthetic experience. I like to think of it as the robot practicing in the Matrix before it ever touches the real world.

The third is the computer on the robot itself, the edge compute, like Jetson Thor, that runs these models in real time with low latency and limited power.

What makes this exciting is that these three pieces form a flywheel. You collect some real-world data, augment it massively in simulation, train a bigger model, deploy it, and that deployment gives you more data. Each turn of the flywheel makes the robot more capable.

As for the future of autonomy, I believe that everything that moves will eventually be autonomous. Cars are the first wave, but humanoids, robot arms in factories, warehouse robots, even everyday devices will follow. Our goal is to be the platform that every robotics company can build on, so they don't have to reinvent the whole stack. It's similar to how CUDA enabled the deep learning revolution. We want to provide the infrastructure layer for physical AI.

I think we're at a moment comparable to the early days of GPT, where the recipe is starting to become clear. The next few years will be about scaling it, and I'm optimistic we'll see a "GPT moment" for robotics sooner than many people expect.

r001.rationale: Describes NVIDIA as a robotics platform built from GPU training infrastructure for foundation models, simulation tools, and edge compute such as Jetson Thor.

r002.rationale: Explicitly predicts that “everything that moves will eventually be autonomous.”

r003.rationale: Does not say intelligent robots could become as numerous as iPhones or use that prospect to argue the platform should be built today.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that robotics is really the last frontier where AI has to leave the screen and touch the physical world, and the hard part is that you can't get there with just one piece. You need the whole stack. So at NVIDIA we're trying to build three computers for robotics. There's the training computer, the big data-center GPUs where you train the foundation model. There's the simulation computer, Omniverse and Isaac Sim, which is really a digital twin of the world where a robot can practice a million lifetimes before it ever moves a motor in reality. And then there's the computer that runs on the robot itself, Jetson, the brain in the body.

Those three have to form a loop. You train in the cloud, you verify and generate data in simulation, you deploy to the edge, and whatever the robot experiences in the real world feeds back into the next round of training. That flywheel is what I think of as the path to autonomy. Language models got to where they are because the internet handed them trillions of tokens for free. Robots don't have that. There's no internet of motor commands. So simulation becomes the data engine, and the GPU is what makes it possible to simulate at a scale where the data starts to look as abundant as text.

The piece I'm most excited about is the model layer on top of that, what we call Project GR00T, a foundation model for humanoid robots. The bet is that the humanoid form factor matters because the world was built for humans, so every kitchen, every factory floor, every warehouse is already training data for a human-shaped body. If you can get one general model that takes in vision and language and outputs actions across many different robot bodies, then you stop writing bespoke code for every task and every machine. That's the transition from the robotics equivalent of expert systems to the robotics equivalent of GPT.

And I'll say the honest part, which is that we're early. We don't yet have the "GPT-3 moment" for robotics where one model suddenly generalizes to things it was never explicitly trained for. But I think the full-stack approach is what gets us there, because no single breakthrough in a model or a chip or a simulator is enough on its own. It's the fact that all of them are co-designed that lets you move fast. My rough prediction is that within a few years, physical AI is going to feel the way language AI felt in 2022, where something clicks and the world realizes it isn't a demo anymore.

r001.rationale: The response describes NVIDIA’s training GPUs, simulation tools, robot-side Jetson computer, and GR00T foundation model as parts of a co-designed full stack.

r002.rationale: It predicts a coming breakthrough in physical AI, but does not say that everything that moves will eventually be autonomous.

r003.rationale: It describes building the robotics platform, but does not mention robots becoming as numerous as iPhones or use that prospect as the reason to start building today.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that robotics isn’t just a model problem. You need a whole loop: generating experience, training a policy, running it on a physical machine, and learning from where it fails. NVIDIA’s full-stack approach brings the compute, simulation, and onboard deployment pieces together.

Simulation is especially exciting because collecting real-world robot experience is slow and expensive. In a virtual world, you can let many robots practice in parallel, vary the environments, and expose them to situations that would be difficult to stage physically. But the real world is still the test. A policy that works beautifully in simulation has to handle imperfect sensors, unexpected contact, and objects it has never seen.

My view is that we’re moving toward more general robot policies—systems that can reuse skills across tasks and, eventually, across different bodies. The platform makes that research loop faster. The long-term opportunity is to make developing an autonomous machine much less bespoke, so each new robot doesn’t have to learn everything from scratch.

r001.rationale: It describes NVIDIA’s full-stack approach as bringing compute, simulation, and onboard deployment together, but does not identify chips and foundation models as parts of a unified platform.

r002.rationale: It predicts more general robot policies and reuse across tasks and bodies, but does not say that everything that moves will eventually be autonomous.

r003.rationale: It describes a long-term opportunity to make autonomous machine development less bespoke, but does not mention robots becoming as numerous as iPhones or use that prospect to argue for building the platform today.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to view robotics as a whole system. A robot needs to perceive the world, reason about what it should do, and turn that reasoning into reliable physical actions. Those pieces have to work together.

A full-stack platform can connect the compute used to train models, the simulation environments where you develop and test them, and the onboard compute that runs them. That creates a feedback loop: you learn from deployment, recreate difficult situations in simulation, improve the model, and bring it back to the robot.

To me, the exciting future is one where we don’t have to engineer every behavior separately. We can build more general capabilities that transfer across tasks and robots. But the real measure of progress is whether those capabilities work reliably in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response connects training compute, models, simulation, and onboard compute, but does not clearly identify chips or foundation models as parts of NVIDIA’s unified platform.

r002.rationale: It discusses general capabilities for robots but does not predict that everything that moves will eventually be autonomous.

r003.rationale: It does not mention robots becoming as numerous as iPhones or argue that this warrants starting to build the platform today.
